reading.h: The 2026 limits table (know the shape, verify the numbers)
reading.body:
These are the tax-year **2026** figures (IRS Notice 2025-67). The IRS indexes the dollar amounts and re-releases them every November. So learn the structure, and treat the exact dollars as annual-verify.

**IRA** (traditional plus Roth combined): **$7,500**, plus a **$1,100** catch-up at 50 or older. **401(k)/403(b)/457(b)/TSP** elective deferral: **$24,500**, plus **$8,000** catch-up at 50 or older (a larger super catch-up of $11,250 at ages 60-63). **415(c)** total defined-contribution addition (employee plus employer): **$72,000**. **SEP**: employer contribution up to 25% of comp, max **$72,000**. **SIMPLE** deferral: **$17,000** (plus $4,000 catch-up). **Defined-benefit** max annual benefit: **$290,000**. Compensation cap: **$360,000**.

One pattern survives the annual reset. The IRA is the smallest bucket. The 401(k)/403(b)/457 family shares one deferral number. And 457(b) sits separate from the others: an employee with a 403(b) and a governmental 457(b) can defer the full amount to **each**.

Anyone with **earned income** can contribute — wages, self-employment, or pre-2019 alimony. Interest, dividends, capital gains, pension, and rental income do **not** count. There is **no age limit** on contributions, and a **spousal IRA** lets a non-working spouse contribute on a joint return.

The deadline is the **tax-filing deadline (April 15), no extensions**. An **excess contribution** is penalized **6% per year** until you remove it. Growth is tax-deferred. Withdrawals are **ordinary income**, with a **10% penalty before age 59½** on the taxable amount.

Some IRA investments are **prohibited**: **life insurance, collectibles, and naked/uncovered options**; margin is barred too. Municipal bonds are legal but **unsuitable**, because you would turn tax-free income into taxable income.

**Required minimum distributions (RMDs)** from traditional, SEP, SIMPLE, and 403(b) accounts begin at age **73** (born 1951-1959) or **75** (born 1960 or later). You may delay the first RMD to **April 1 of the year after** you turn 73, but then you take two that year. A missed RMD is penalized **25%**, cut to **10%** if you fix it within two years.

A **Roth IRA** owner has **no lifetime RMDs**. A Roth **qualified (tax-free) distribution** needs **both**: (a) **5 tax years** since the first Roth contribution, and (b) a trigger — age 59½, death, disability, or first-home purchase ($10,000 lifetime). **Ordering rules**: withdrawals come out contributions first (always tax- and penalty-free), then conversions, then earnings.

A **direct (trustee-to-trustee) transfer** is unlimited, with no tax and no withholding. The money never touches the participant.

An **indirect rollover** pays the participant, who must redeposit within **60 days**. Two catches. IRA-to-IRA indirect rollovers are limited to **one per 12 months**. And a distribution from a **qualified plan** paid to the participant carries **mandatory 20% federal withholding**.

Worked example: a 45-year-old asks for her $100,000 401(k) paid to her. She receives **$80,000** (20% withheld). To roll over the full $100,000, she must add **$20,000 from other funds** within 60 days. If she deposits only the $80,000, the missing **$20,000 is a taxable distribution** plus a **10% penalty** ($2,000) at her age. The withholding is only a credit against her tax bill.

reading.h: The plan zoo: who sponsors, who funds
reading.body:
**SEP IRA** — **employer-funded only** (no employee deferrals); up to 25% of comp; covers employees 21 or older who worked **3 of the last 5 years**; **immediate 100% vesting**. **SIMPLE** — for employers with **100 employees or fewer** and no other plan; the employer must **match up to 3%** or make a **2% non-elective** contribution; a **25% penalty** (not 10%) applies to withdrawals in the first 2 years.

**401(k)** — elective deferrals plus optional match, vesting schedules on employer money, loans up to **50% of vested balance or $50,000 max**. **403(b)/TSA** — public schools and 501(c)(3)s; investments limited to **annuities and mutual funds**. **457(b)** — state and local governments and tax-exempts; the limit is **separate** from 401(k)/403(b), and **governmental 457(b) withdrawals carry no 10% penalty** at any age. **Keogh (HR-10)** — for self-employed or unincorporated businesses.

**Defined benefit** promises a formula benefit; the employer bears the risk, and the PBGC insures it. **Defined contribution** defines the input, and the **employee bears the risk**.

The **10% early-withdrawal penalty** (before 59½) is waived for the classic list the exam tests: **death; total and permanent disability; substantially equal periodic payments (72(t)/SEPP); unreimbursed medical expenses over 7.5% of AGI; an IRS levy**; and, **IRA-only**, a **first-time home purchase ($10,000 lifetime)** and **qualified higher-education expenses**. From employer plans only, **separation from service in or after the year you turn 55** (the Rule of 55) and **QDRO** payments also escape the penalty.

Note the split. First-home and education waivers are **IRA-only**. The age-55 separation waiver is **employer-plan-only**.

A **Coverdell ESA** allows a small yearly contribution (**$2,000** per beneficiary, not indexed) from after-tax money. It has **contributor income limits**, requires contributions to stop at age **18**, and must be **used or rolled to a family member by age 30**. It covers K-12 and higher education.

A **529 plan** is a **municipal fund security** sold with a disclosure document. It has **no federal income limit** on contributors and much higher contribution room. A 529 **contribution is a gift**, so it uses the annual gift exclusion or a **5-year election** (front-loading five years of exclusions at once). The owner keeps control and can change the beneficiary to a **family member** tax-free. Earnings are federally tax-free for qualified education expenses. A non-qualified withdrawal is taxed on earnings plus a **10% penalty**. SECURE 2.0 even allows a lifetime **$35,000 529-to-Roth rollover** once the account is 15 years old.

flashcards.front: Which income qualifies you to contribute to an IRA?
flashcards.back: Earned income (wages, self-employment, pre-2019 alimony). Not interest, dividends, capital gains, pension, or rental income.

flashcards.front: IRA contribution deadline and excess penalty
flashcards.back: Tax-filing deadline (April 15), no extensions. An excess contribution is penalized 6% per year until removed.
73 for those born 1951-1959; 75 for those born 1960 or later. A Roth IRA owner has no lifetime RMDs.
5 tax years since the first Roth contribution, and a trigger (59½, death, disability, or first home $10,000).
Contributions first (always tax- and penalty-free), then conversions, then earnings.
60 days to redeposit; IRA-to-IRA limited to one per 12 months; a qualified-plan distribution to the participant has mandatory 20% withholding.

flashcards.front: SEP IRA — who funds, eligibility, vesting
flashcards.back: Employer-funded only (no employee deferrals); covers those 21 or older who worked 3 of the last 5 years; immediate 100% vesting.
100 employees or fewer, no other plan; employer match up to 3% or 2% non-elective; 25% penalty (not 10%) on withdrawals in the first 2 years.
No 10% early-withdrawal penalty at any age. Its deferral limit is separate from 401(k)/403(b).
IRA-only: first home ($10k), higher education. Employer-plan-only: separation from service at or after age 55 (Rule of 55), QDRO.

529: no federal income limit, high contribution room, treated as a gift, muni fund security. Coverdell: $2,000/yr, income-limited, contribute until 18, use by 30.

quiz.stem: An employer matches 100% of an employee's 401(k) contributions up to 4% of salary. An employee earning $50,000 contributes exactly 4% of salary this year. Before any investment gains, how much goes into the account for the year?
options: $2,000, because the match is paid only at retirement
$2,080, because the employer adds 4% of the $2,000 contribution
$4,000, the employee's $2,000 plus a $2,000 employer match
$6,000, because the employer contributes 4% of salary plus a matching $2,000
quiz.explanation: 4% of $50,000 = $2,000 from the employee; a 100% match up to 4% adds another $2,000, for $4,000 total. The match is an immediate dollar-for-dollar addition, not a percentage of the employee's contribution.

quiz.stem: Which of the following accounts does NOT require the original owner to take required minimum distributions during his or her lifetime?
options: Traditional IRA
SEP IRA
Roth IRA
403(b) plan
quiz.explanation: A Roth IRA owner has no lifetime RMDs (beneficiaries do). Traditional, SEP, and 403(b) accounts all require RMDs beginning at age 73 (75 for those born in 1960 or later).

quiz.stem: A 45-year-old leaves her employer and asks that her $100,000 401(k) balance be paid directly to her. She receives a check for $80,000 and, within 60 days, deposits that $80,000 into a rollover IRA. The tax result is:
options: No tax is due; the $20,000 withheld is refunded in full when she files
The entire $100,000 is taxable because only a direct transfer avoids tax
$20,000 is taxable as ordinary income and is subject to a 10% early-withdrawal penalty
$20,000 is taxable, but no penalty applies because the plan withheld it
quiz.explanation: A plan distribution paid to the participant carries mandatory 20% withholding ($20,000). To roll over the full $100,000 she had to replace that $20,000 from other money; the amount not redeposited is a taxable distribution plus, at age 45, a 10% penalty. The withholding is merely a credit against her total tax.

quiz.stem: Under current rules, an individual born in 1955 must begin taking required minimum distributions from a traditional IRA at age:
quiz.explanation: For those born 1951-1959 the required beginning age is 73; age 75 applies only to those born in 1960 or later. The old 70½ and interim 72 ages no longer apply after SECURE 2.0.

quiz.stem: A distribution of earnings from a Roth IRA is tax-free (qualified) only if the account has met the 5-year holding requirement AND one of the following. Which one?
options: The owner has reached age 55 and separated from service
The owner is at least 59½, or the distribution is due to death, disability, or a first-home purchase
The owner has stopped making new contributions
The distribution is rolled into another Roth within 60 days
quiz.explanation: A qualified Roth distribution requires both the 5-tax-year clock and a qualifying event: age 59½, death, disability, or a first-home purchase ($10,000 lifetime). The Rule of 55 is an employer-plan penalty exception, not a Roth qualified-distribution trigger.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of a SEP IRA?
options: It is funded entirely by the employer; employees make no salary-deferral contributions
Employees may defer part of their salary, and the employer must match dollar-for-dollar
It is available only to employers with more than 100 employees
Contributions vest on a 3-year cliff schedule
quiz.explanation: A SEP is employer-funded only — there are no employee elective deferrals — and contributions are immediately 100% vested. Salary deferrals and matching describe a 401(k) or SIMPLE, not a SEP.

quiz.stem: A single taxpayer under age 59½ takes an early withdrawal from her traditional IRA. Which use of the funds is NOT among the exceptions that avoid the 10% early-withdrawal penalty?
options: A first-time home purchase up to $10,000
Qualified higher-education expenses
The purchase of a new automobile for commuting to work
Total and permanent disability
quiz.explanation: A first-time home purchase, higher-education expenses, and disability are recognized exceptions; buying a car is not. The car purchase is an ordinary personal expense and does not waive the 10% penalty.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a 529 plan from a Coverdell ESA?
options: A 529 plan imposes a federal income limit on contributors; a Coverdell does not
A 529 plan has no federal income limit on contributors and allows much larger contributions than a Coverdell
A Coverdell allows a 5-year gift election; a 529 does not
A Coverdell has no age limits, while a 529 must be used by age 30
quiz.explanation: A 529 has no federal income limit on contributors and far higher contribution room, and a contribution is treated as a gift (eligible for the 5-year election). The Coverdell is the one with contributor income limits, a small annual cap, and age limits (contribute until 18, use by 30).
